narrative:
Einstein's theory of relativity emerged in two distinct stages across a decade of work. In 1905 he published the Special Theory of Relativity, establishing that the speed of light is constant regardless of the observer [[1]]. This foundational insight reshaped the relationship between space and time, treating them not as independent absolutes but as a unified fabric.

Ten years later, in 1915, Einstein extended his thinking to encompass gravity itself, producing the General Theory of Relativity [[1]]. Where Newton had described gravity as a force acting at a distance, Einstein recast it as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass [[1]]. Objects do not pull on one another so much as they warp the geometry through which everything moves.

The consequences of this geometric picture are measurable and strange. Massive objects bend the path of light and cause time itself to run more slowly in their vicinity [[2]]. These predictions — once considered almost philosophically extravagant — placed relativity among the most empirically tested frameworks in the history of physics.
